content.title: 2026 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guideline
content.narrative_summary: Prompt diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism (PE) requires recognition of predisposing risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) and integration of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and imaging. PE symptoms are nonspecific; the most common are pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, while hemoptysis, syncope, and shock are less common. Physical findings such as tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxemia, decreased breath sounds, pleural friction rub, jugular venous distension, and signs of deep vein thrombosis may indicate PE, but diagnosis is often challenging with fewer than 10% of evaluated patients ultimately diagnosed. Pretest probability scores (e.g., Wells score, Revised Geneva score, Pulmonary Embolism Rule Out Criteria) guide appropriate investigations.

rows.recommendation: 2. In adult patients undergoing evaluation for PE and who have a low or intermediate clinical probability of PE (<50%) by risk assessment, an age‐adjusted D‐dimer value below the threshold (age × 10 μg/L for fibrinogen equivalent units assays) effectively excludes PE and the need for imaging.2-5
3. In adult patients with suspected PE, the YEARS algorithm* can be useful to identify which patients do not need imaging to rule out a PE.2,3,6,7
4. In pregnant adults, it may be reasonable to use pregnancy‐adapted YEARS criteria to identify patients who do not need imaging for PE.8-10

content.title: 3.1.2 Diagnostic Testing
content.narrative_summary: Continued discussion of D-dimer thresholds and diagnostic strategies for pulmonary embolism. A prospective validation of 3,346 patients showed low failure rates using age-adjusted D-dimer and clinical probability thresholds. Meta-analyses and multicenter trials confirmed safety of age-adjusted D-dimer and the YEARS algorithm across probability levels using thresholds of 500 µg/L and 1,000 µg/L. In pregnant patients, CTPA detection rates are low, and diagnostic strategies using quantitative D-dimer with adjusted algorithms demonstrated low failure rates.

rows.recommendation: In patients presenting with symptoms and signs suggestive of acute PE, imaging is recommended for those who are deemed high probability (>50% probability of PE) by a validated clinical risk prediction score or an elevated D-dimer level in order to confirm or exclude PE.
In patients undergoing imaging evaluation for suspected PE, a positive CTPA or high probability ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is sufficient to diagnose PE.
In patients undergoing imaging evaluation, a CTPA is recommended in preference to a V/Q scan to confirm the diagnosis of acute PE.

In pregnant patients presenting with symptoms, YEARS criteria suggestive of acute PE, and a normal chest x-ray, imaging evaluation with low-radiation dose CTPA is reasonable over low-dose perfusion scintigraphy.
In patients undergoing evaluation for PE, V/Q single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is reasonable in preference to a planar V/Q scan as a diagnostic study.

In patients with suspected acute PE who cannot undergo a CTPA, it is reasonable to perform a V/Q scan in preference to contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) to improve the diagnostic yield.

content.narrative_summary: Imaging is essential to the diagnosis and management of patients with PE and must be placed within the context of pretest probability. CTPA is the standard modality given its accessibility, cost, and performance; when CTPA is not possible, V/Q scan is appropriate. Echocardiography is inadequate to diagnose PE but important for assessing RV function (RV/LV ratio, diameters, TAPSE, systolic pressure, free wall hypokinesis, tricuspid velocity, septal motion, and IVC collapse). RV dysfunction should be reported on CTPA when PE is confirmed. Venous duplex ultrasound may be useful in patients with clinical findings suggestive of DVT or when DVT confirmation will influence management.

rows.recommendation: 7. In patients with confirmed acute PE, obtaining lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound examination may be reasonable in patients with clinical findings suggestive of DVT or if the presence of DVT will change management or inform prognosis.
8. In patients with suspected PE and a negative CTPA or normal V/Q SPECT, venous duplex ultrasonography is not useful for further PE diagnostic evaluation.
9. In patients with suspected acute PE, an echocardiogram is not recommended to confirm or refute the diagnosis of PE.

10. In patients with suspected acute PE, computed tomographic venography of the inferior vena cava (IVC) and lower extremity veins is not recommended as a routine adjunct to CTPA to diagnose venous thrombosis.

11. In patients presenting with an acute PE who undergo CTPA, reporting the numerical right ventricle (RV)/left ventricle (LV) ratio (measured by internal diameter assessed on axial or reformatted 4D-chamber view) is recommended over subjective quantification for risk stratification.

12. In patients with acute PE who undergo transthoracic echocardiography, RV dysfunction should be assessed and reported by the following parameters: RV/LV end-diastolic ratio; RV end-diastolic diameter; tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE); estimated right ventricular systolic pressure; RV free wall hypokinesis with sparing of the apex (McConnell’s sign); tricuspid systolic velocity; paradoxical septal motion; and IVC respirophasic collapse to assist with risk stratification.
13. In patients with acute PE, reporting of chronic features* on CTPA may be useful to identify patients at risk for chronic clinical sequelae of PE, including post-PE CTEPD.

content.title: 2026 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guideline
content.narrative_summary: This page continues a discussion of imaging strategies for the evaluation of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). It covers: 1) the diagnostic performance and follow-up outcomes of negative CTPA, including low recurrence rates and the limited utility of adjunctive duplex ultrasonography when CTPA is negative; 2) the limited sensitivity of echocardiography alone to confirm or exclude PE and its improved performance only in hemodynamically compromised patients; 3) the role of computed tomographic venography (CTV) of the inferior vena cava and lower extremity veins in detecting deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and its predictive values versus duplex ultrasonography; 4) the importance of reporting RV/LV ratio and other RV strain parameters on CTPA rather than subjective assessment; 5) comprehensive echocardiographic evaluation of RV dysfunction and strain parameters by trained operators; and 6) the identification of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) and measurement of pulmonary venous flow reduction (PVFR) on CTPA for long-term risk stratification.

content.narrative_summary: Cardiac biomarkers (troponin and BNP) are important tools incorporated into clinical risk tools to identify patients with acute PE at risk for short-term complications and mortality. Lactate is an additional risk marker, particularly among normotensive patients with acute symptomatic PE, where it may indicate subclinical end-organ hypoperfusion. Elevated lactate correlates with early complications and mortality and provides incremental data beyond cardiac biomarkers alone. Lactate levels have been used to guide the selection of advanced therapies. Arterial or venous lactate should be measured whenever cardiac biomarkers are assessed for risk stratification, with thresholds based on the local assay.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Risk Stratification of PE Using Biomarkers

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute PE and an elevated clinical severity score without features of hypotension or shock (ie, AHA/ACC PE Category C), measurement of at least 1 cardiac biomarker (ie, troponin, brain natriuretic peptide [BNP]) is recommended to assist with risk stratification for short-term complications and/or mortality.

In patients with acute PE AHA/ACC PE Categories C to E who are undergoing evaluation at an acute care facility, measurement of lactate (either venous or arterial) is recommended to assist with risk stratification for short-term complications and/or mortality.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of biomarker prognostic studies, noting that elevated troponin, BNP, and lactate levels are associated with increased all-cause and PE-related mortality. The Synopsis emphasizes that RV imaging is recommended for risk stratification in patients with acute symptomatic PE and elevated clinical severity scores.

section_headings: 3.2.5. Quantification of Thrombus Burden for Short-Term Risk Stratification
4.1.1. Suitability for Outpatient Management of PE
content.narrative_summary: Under section 3.2.5, the guideline explains that although chest CT can quantify thromboembolic volume and angiographic obstruction, current data do not support using measures of thrombus burden (eg, modified Miller score) for short-term risk stratification or determining reperfusion therapy. Anatomic characterization may inform feasibility and safety of advanced therapies. Under section 4, anticoagulation with DOACs or LMWH is the foundation of acute PE management. Further strategies including biomarker measurement, RV imaging, hemodynamic assessment, and use of a multidisciplinary PERT are guided by individual risk factors. In 4.1.1, outpatient treatment of acute PE using validated decision tools (eg, Hestia, PESI, sPESI) varies by region and patient risk, with evidence showing similar clinical outcomes to inpatient care when rates of adverse events are low.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Quantification of Thrombus Burden for Short-Term Risk Stratification

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC PE Categories A-C, quantification of angiographic thrombus burden for short-term risk stratification is not recommended.1-4

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Suitability for Outpatient Management of PE

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients diagnosed with acute PE in a clinic or an ED, it is reasonable to use a decision tool* to identify suitability for outpatient treatment.1

2. In select patients diagnosed with acute PE in AHA ACC PE Categories A and B in a clinic or ED, outpatient treatment† is a reasonable option compared with hospitalization, when the rate of 90-day adverse outcomes is low and it aligns with patient goals.2

content.narrative_summary: Studies show that PERTs reduce the time to therapeutic anticoagulation and decrease the use of IVC filters, with reductions in hospital and ICU length of stay in most studies. The impact on mortality is mixed, with some studies showing decreased rates and others showing no change. Overall, PERTs improve clinical outcomes in several areas, but their effect on mortality is not yet conclusively established.

content.narrative_summary: The model and process of PERT activation are described. When a pulmonary embolism (PE) is diagnosed, the designated in-house PERT physician is paged, pertinent clinical information is gathered, and the severity of the case is assessed. If necessary, members of a multidisciplinary team discuss the case via phone, virtual meeting, or in person. Diagnostic and treatment options are discussed, recommendations are generated, and appropriate resources are mobilized. Upon discharge, patients follow up in a multidisciplinary clinic. COR indicates class of recommendation; PE, pulmonary embolism; PERT, pulmonary embolism response team.

rows.recommendation: 2. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC Categories C1–E1 who require parenteral anticoagulant therapy initially, LMWH is recommended over UFH to reduce recurrent VTE and major bleeding.2

5. In patients with obesity (body mass index [BMI] >30 kg/m2) and acute PE who are receiving oral anticoagulant therapy, treatment with a DOAC (unless contraindicated) over a VKA is reasonable to prevent recurrent PE and reduce major bleeding.5–10
6. In patients with class III obesity (BMI >40 kg/m2) and acute PE who are receiving LMWH therapy, reducing the dose of LMWH may be reasonable to reduce the risk of bleeding.11,12
7. In patients with acute PE and established thrombotic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, a VKA is recommended in preference to a DOAC for the prevention of venous and arterial thrombosis.13–16
8. In patients with acute PE determined to have only a single anticardiolipin antibody or a β2-glycoprotein antibody, a DOAC might be a reasonable alternative to a VKA to prevent recurrent PE.13–15
9. In patients with primary or metastatic brain tumors and acute PE who are otherwise eligible for oral anticoagulation, a DOAC may be considered over LMWH to reduce the risk of ICH.17–19
10. In patients with mild-to-moderate (stage 2–3) chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute PE who require oral anticoagulant therapy, a DOAC is recommended over a VKA to reduce major bleeding.20–22

11. In patients with severe kidney disease (stage 4–5) or endstage kidney disease on hemodialysis and confirmed PE who require oral anticoagulant therapy, it is uncertain whether apixaban is better than VKA to reduce major bleeding.23,24
12. In patients who are pregnant, have acute PE, and can receive anticoagulation, either LMWH or UFH are recommended to prevent recurrent VTE.25
13. In patients who are pregnant and have acute PE, DOACs and warfarin are potentially harmful and may result in miscarriages or fetal anomalies.26
14. In patients with acute PE who are breastfeeding and require anticoagulation, LMWH, UFH, or warfarin are recommended over a DOAC, to prevent potential bleeding in the infant.26,27
15. In patients with Child-Pugh class A chronic liver disease and acute PE, treatment with a DOAC instead of a VKA is reasonable to reduce bleeding.28

content.narrative_summary: Anticoagulation is the mainstay of therapy for confirmed acute PE. DOACs are preferred for long-term management due to efficacy, ease of use, and lower bleeding risk compared with VKAs. For initial parenteral therapy, LMWH is recommended over UFH because of reduced recurrent VTE and fewer complications like heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Specific populations—including those with obesity, CKD, liver disease, pregnancy, and thrombophilia—require tailored dosing strategies or avoidance of certain agents (e.g., DOACs and VKAs in pregnancy and breastfeeding; VKAs preferred in antiphospholipid syndrome). Shared decision-making is essential for patients with severe renal or hepatic impairment.

rows.recommendation: In patients with Child-Pugh class B chronic liver disease and acute PE, treatment with a DOAC instead of a VKA may be reasonable to reduce bleeding risk.
In patients with Child-Pugh class C chronic liver disease and acute PE, treatment with a DOAC instead of a VKA is not recommended due to potential for increased bleeding.
In patients with acute PE undergoing CDL, concurrent therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH or UFH) or subtherapeutic anticoagulation (UFH) is recommended over no anticoagulation to prevent recurrent PE.

In patients with acute PE who have undergone an endovascular procedure or received thrombolytic therapy, initial parenteral anticoagulation with LMWH is preferred over UFH to provide reliable therapeutic anticoagulation and reduce the risk of recurrent VTE.
In patients with acute PE likely to undergo endovascular procedures for PE management, LMWH is reasonable over UFH to provide more effective anticoagulation.

In patients with acute PE in whom LMWH is monitored, measuring a peak anti-Xa level 3 to 5 hours after an LMWH dose once a steady state is reached (≥3 doses) is recommended in preference to checking trough or random levels in order to most accurately identify if the patient is within the expected therapeutic range.

In patients with acute PE who have severe CKD (CrCl of <30 mL/min) and are being treated with LMWH, it is reasonable to monitor anti-Xa levels to guide dose adjustment in order to reduce bleeding risk.

In pregnant patients treated with LMWH for acute PE, the usefulness of monitoring the peak anti-Xa level at least once per trimester is not well established to guide dose adjustment and reduce bleeding and/or thromboembolic risk.

In patients who weigh >150 kg or have a BMI of >40 kg/m2 and are receiving LMWH for treatment of acute PE, the benefit of monitoring anti-Xa levels is not established to avoid supratherapeutic levels of LMWH after initial therapy.
In patients with acute PE treated with LMWH in the ICU, the benefit of monitoring anti-Xa levels is not established to avoid supratherapeutic and/or subtherapeutic levels.
In most patients with acute PE treated with weight-based LMWH, laboratory monitoring of anti-Xa level and dose adjustment is not indicated to reduce recurrent VTE or bleeding.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Inferior Vena Cava Filters

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with acute PE who cannot tolerate anticoagulation but in whom an IVC filter is deemed necessary, retrievable IVC filters are recommended over permanent filters to reduce the short-term incidence of recurrent PE while minimizing long-term adverse outcomes.

2. In patients with retrievable IVC filters, retrieval should be attempted as soon as the risk of PE has sufficiently decreased and anticoagulation tolerated in order to minimize the risk of long-term filter-related complications.
3. In patients with acute PE who cannot tolerate anticoagulation, IVC filters can be useful to reduce the short-term incidence of recurrent PE.
4. In patients with indwelling IVC filters, the use of a structured follow-up program is reasonable to increase retrieval rates and detect complications.

5. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC PE Categories D-E, and who are undergoing advanced interventions such as systemic thrombolysis, CDL, MT, or surgical embolectomy, the benefit of IVC filter placement is uncertain to reduce the short-term incidence of recurrent PE and mortality.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that inferior vena cava (IVC) filters mechanically intercept venous thrombi migrating to the pulmonary circulation, available in permanent and retrievable forms, and discusses their evolving clinical utility, particularly when anticoagulation is contraindicated or recurrent PE occurs despite treatment. The recommendation-specific supportive text reviews trials (PREPIC, PREPIC2) and meta-analyses demonstrating higher rates of DVT and no long-term survival benefit with filters, emphasizes minimizing dwell time and favoring retrievable filters, and underscores the importance of timely filter retrieval to reduce complications, with data showing increased retrieval difficulty after 50–90 days.

rows.recommendation: 6. In patients with recurrent PE despite optimal therapeutic anticoagulation who are in AHA/ACC PE Categories B–E, IVC filter placement may be considered to reduce the short-term incidence of additional recurrent PE.¹,²,4,12
7. In patients with acute PE who are therapeutically anticoagulated, routine IVC filter placement should not be performed.⁵–⁸

content.title: 4.4. Advanced Management
content.narrative_summary: Free-floating intracardiac clot-in-transit occurs in 2–4% of acute PE cases and has historically been managed with a variety of strategies including anticoagulation alone, surgical embolectomy, systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed lysis (CDL), and mechanical thrombectomy (MT). High-quality comparative data are lacking. Ongoing cardiovascular outcome trials are evaluating CDL versus MT in AHA/ACC PE Categories C2-D2, and multiple clinical and anatomical factors guide therapy choice.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC PE Categories C3-E2 who have evidence of free-floating right atrial and/or RV clot-in-transit, the utilization of advanced therapies over anticoagulation alone is reasonable to reduce the risk of clinical deterioration.

2. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC PE Categories C2-D2 and without contraindications to thrombolysis, and in whom advanced therapy is being considered, the usefulness of either CDL or MT over the other is uncertain for reduction in mortality or major bleeding.

1. In patients with acute PE in AHA/ACC PE Categories E1-2 and acceptable bleeding risk, in whom advanced therapy is being considered, systemic thrombolysis and anticoagulation is reasonable over anticoagulation alone to reduce mortality and recurrent PE.

content.narrative_summary: Four small randomized controlled trials (total n=224) in high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) patients showed systemic thrombolysis plus anticoagulation improved pulmonary obstruction and right ventricular dilation compared with heparin alone, but with increased risk of bleeding (including intracranial hemorrhage). The FDA has approved three thrombolytic agents (streptokinase, urokinase, rt-PA) for PE, though head-to-head superiority is not established. Tenecteplase has been studied off-label. Standard rt-PA dosing (100 mg over 2 h) is most commonly used. Meta-analyses suggest modest mortality benefit but higher bleeding risk, particularly in hemodynamically unstable or decompensating patients, and lower‐dose regimens may reduce bleeding.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Follow-Up Care for Acute PE

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute PE, it is beneficial to have clinical follow-up within the first week of discharge to provide patient education, address barriers to anticoagulation therapy, ensure adherence to prescribed medications, and detect bleeding complications.

Patients with acute PE should have a clinical visit at or before 3 months after diagnosis to discuss duration of anticoagulation, review the need for further testing, and assess for persistent PE-related symptoms.

Patients who have had acute PE should be asked about PE-related symptoms and functional limitations at every visit for at least 1 year to screen for CTEPD or other causes of dyspnea and functional limitation.

In patients with a history of acute PE who remain on anticoagulation into the extended phase (beyond 3-6 months from diagnosis), periodic reassessment of the risk and benefits of continued anticoagulation is recommended to ensure the safety and efficacy of continuing anticoagulation.
In patients with acute PE, the use of general or disease-specific questionnaires is reasonable to screen for anxiety and depression at follow-up visits.
In select complex patients* with acute PE, it is reasonable to have follow-up care occur in a specialized PE clinic, if available, to optimize care.

In patients who remain symptomatic 3 to 6 months after acute PE, it may be reasonable to obtain a performance test (six-minute walk test, incremental shuttle walk test, endurance shuttle walk test) to quantify physical limitations and identify which patients require more extensive evaluation.

section_headings: 6.1. Persistently Symptomatic Patients After Acute PE
content.narrative_summary: Up to half of patients after acute PE have ongoing dyspnea or functional impairment despite ≥3 months of anticoagulation; about half have residual pulmonary vascular obstruction on imaging (RPVO). CTEPD includes those with persistent symptoms, RPVO, and vascular disease–related exercise limitation, with or without resting PH. CTEPD with PH (CTEPH) occurs in ~3% of acute PE patients, and CTEPD without PH is at least as prevalent. Diagnostic evaluation of symptomatic patients at ≥3 months aims to determine etiology and exclude CTEPD; a diagnostic algorithm is shown in Figure 8.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Persistently Symptomatic Patients After Acute PE

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with ongoing dyspnea and/or functional impairment after ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation after an acute PE, a diagnostic evaluation is recommended to assess for CTEPD.

2. For patients undergoing a diagnostic evaluation for CTEPD, it is reasonable to obtain both a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE)* and a lung perfusion scan (planar V/Q, or V/Q single-photon emission CT [SPECT], SPECT/CT) over an echocardiogram alone to exclude CTEPD or determine if additional diagnostic testing is needed.
3. For patients undergoing a diagnostic evaluation for CTEPD, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is reasonable to exclude CTEPD.

4. In patients with a history of acute PE, who have resolution of symptoms and low suspicion for CTEPD, a follow-up CTPA or lung perfusion scan (planar V/Q, V/Q SPECT, SPECT/CT) is not beneficial to assess for the degree of thrombosis resolution.

5. Patients being evaluated for CTEPD should continue anticoagulation until the evaluation is completed to prevent recurrent VTE and/or CTEPD progression unless contraindicated due to high bleeding risk.

6. For patients in whom CTEPD has been excluded but who have ongoing dyspnea and/or functional impairment despite ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation after an acute PE, a pulmonary rehabilitation program is reasonable to improve symptoms and exercise tolerance.
7. For patients with a diagnosis of CTEPD with PH, referral to a center with expertise in managing CTEPD is recommended to optimize evaluation and management.
8. For select patients with a diagnosis of CTEPD without PH, referral to a center with expertise can be beneficial in managing CTEPD.

content.narrative_summary: Supports Recommendation 1 by summarizing prospective studies (InShape II and FOCUS) showing that performing diagnostic evaluation at 3 months post–acute pulmonary embolism in symptomatic patients reduces time to diagnosis of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease with pulmonary hypertension (CTEPD with PH), and noting that vascular obstruction does not change after 3 months, so delaying evaluation only postpones diagnosis.

content.narrative_summary: Point 2 discusses the limited sensitivity of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for diagnosing chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD), noting that many patients with normal TTEs have abnormal perfusion studies or exercise testing and that combined SPECT/CT and V/Q imaging perform similarly to planar V/Q. Point 3 describes dyspnea and exercise limitation in CTEPD attributable to increased right ventricular afterload and alveolar dead space, and outlines the role of cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) measures such as reduced peak oxygen consumption and elevated ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VCO₂) and dead space (VD/VT). Point 4 summarizes cohort and meta-analysis data showing that residual perfusion defects on CTPA are not predictive of exercise limitation at 12 months and that CTPA has limited utility for follow-up, except in select patients. Point 5 recommends continued anticoagulation in CTEPD patients after an initial event, even if provoking factors are transient, unless bleeding risk is high. Point 6 notes limited randomized trial data on exercise rehabilitation after acute PE, citing one RCT showing improved exercise capacity and quality of life but noting other trials are ongoing.

content.narrative_summary: A study of 184 inoperable CTEPH patients undergoing 1006 BPA sessions showed complication rates decrease significantly from 13.3% to 5.9% (P<0.001). Data on CTEPD without PH are limited to small case series demonstrating improved exercise capacity, functional class, and hemodynamics, suggesting referral to an experienced CTEPD center may benefit some patients, though those with mild disease and CTEPD without PH may have a benign prognosis. Significant evidence gaps in acute PE management include refining risk stratification (eg, validating AHA/ACC categories and integrating novel predictors like thrombus burden and RV metrics), developing safer antithrombotic and thrombolytic therapies, optimizing travel prophylaxis, creating robust comparative-effectiveness algorithms for catheter-based and surgical interventions in high-risk populations, and understanding long-term outcomes in chronic thromboembolic disease and special populations (rural patients, hormone therapy–dependent, pregnant). Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and radiomics show promise for diagnosis and personalized care but require validation. Addressing these gaps is essential to optimize outcomes and tailor treatment strategies for diverse patient populations.

Three categories of echocardiographic signs suggestive of pulmonary hypertension: A: Ventricles; B: Pulmonary Artery; C: Inferior Vena Cava and RA.

- Inferior Vena Cava and RA: IVC diameter >21 mm with decreased inspiratory collapse (<50% with sniff or <20% with quiet inspiration); RA area (end-systole) >18 cm2; (no third-row entry)
